extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in string theory and its criticisms
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating string theory as a theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the evaluative criteria and standards (scientific, conceptual, mathematical, and sociological) that appear in a broad Wikipedia article on string theory, especially in its 'Criticism' and conceptual sections. Useful for judging how well string theory meets various expectations for a successful physical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive power / empirical predictivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory can make testable predictions and thus be used to predict anything at low energies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peter Woit argues that the large number of different vacuum states 'probably destroys the hope of using the theory to predict anything' and that a theory that is 'vacuous and incapable of predicting anything' fails as a scientific framework. The page frames predictivity as central to judging string theory's value for constructing particle-physics models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of solutions (landscape) and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: How many distinct vacuum states the theory admits and whether that plurality undermines its usefulness for unique physical predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that specifying shapes for extra dimensions leads to an enormous number of vacuum states (typically estimated ~10^500), and critics argue this large number can render the theory effectively unconstrained — able to 'accommodate almost any phenomenon' and thereby reduce predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anthropic reasoning / explanatory non-tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether invoking the anthropic principle yields substantive scientific explanation or amounts to a tautological 'excuse for failure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains the anthropic principle and records both proponents (e.g., Weinberg, Susskind) who use it to explain small cosmological constant values and critics (e.g., Woit) who say 'in this case [anthropic reasoning] is nothing more than an excuse for failure.' The entry highlights concerns that anthropic explanations may not be genuinely predictive or explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with observed cosmology / dark energy (positive cosmological constant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory can accommodate a metastable, positive cosmological constant as suggested by Λ-CDM and observations of dark energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states 'It remains unknown whether string theory is compatible with a metastable, positive cosmological constant' and references constructions (e.g., Kachru et al. 2003) and later conjectures that challenge the existence of such vacua. Compatibility with observed dark energy is presented as a concrete empirical constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory is formulated without privileging a particular spacetime geometry (a desideratum drawn from general relativity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that one fundamental property of general relativity is background independence and records Lee Smolin's criticism that string theory 'is not manifestly background-independent' because it typically begins with a fixed reference geometry. Responses (e.g., Polchinski) argue the physics can be background-independent even if the mathematical language is not, and AdS/CFT is cited as progress toward this issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-perturbative completeness / well-defined formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory admits a fully non-perturbative definition (not just a perturbative expansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that matrix theory provided 'the first definition of string theory that was fully non-perturbative' and that discovering D-branes helped resolve perturbative divergences, suggesting non-perturbative formulations are important criteria for theoretical completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to established physics (gauge theories, QCD, hadrons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the theory connects to and informs existing, empirically successful theories like quantum chromodynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that through relationships like AdS/CFT, string theory has been shown to be related to gauge theories such as QCD, leading to a more quantitative understanding of hadrons — presented as a positive evaluative point for relevance to known physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to account for black hole physics and holography
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory explains black-hole entropy, horizon degrees of freedom, and implements the holographic principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents work (e.g., Strominger & Vafa) showing agreement with semi-classical black-hole entropy and describes how the holographic principle and AdS/CFT give concrete realizations linking gravity and gauge theories; success here is treated as significant evidence in favor of the theory's conceptual reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical richness, internal consistency, and fruitful structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the theory exhibits deep mathematical structure (mirror symmetry, conformal field theory, etc.) and yields rigorous mathematical results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly mentions 'rich mathematical structure', rigorous results (e.g., proofs of mirror symmetry), and productive mathematical connections (vertex operator algebras, noncommutative geometry). This mathematical fruitfulness is presented as an evaluative dimension separate from direct empirical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific health: diversity of approaches and avoidance of bandwagon effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the research ecosystem encourages multiple viable approaches (rather than convergence on a single dominant paradigm driven by sociology, funding, or bandwagon effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociological criticisms are recorded: remarks by David Gross that 'there are no other good ideas around', Penrose and Smolin's comments on 'bandwagon effects' and the allocation of resources, and prescriptions to encourage greater diversity of approaches. The article treats the health of the field as a meta-criterion for evaluating string theory research practices.
